title: The Bhatts
hook: court poets whose swayyas praise the Gurus as one light (Swayye, ang 1389–1409)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhikhan asked the Lord to be his physician. Your line was the name as medicine. Did you take a quiet minute when a worry flared? Day seven hundred ninety-one.

A wedding toast. Somebody stands, clinks a glass, and praises the couple. Good toasts are a craft: specific, warm, a little bit grand. Now take people whose whole trade was that craft, praising the great for a living, and send them into the court of the Gurus. That's who the Bhatts were, as tradition tells it: bards, poets of praise. Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, from Ang 1389, their verses fill page after page.
screen: `A TOAST IS A CRAFT.` → `BARDS WHO PRAISED FOR A LIVING.` → `THEIR VERSES NEAR THE END OF THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: Their verses are called swayye, after the swayya, a form of poem, and they're grouped by Guru: swayye for the first Guru, for the second, and on through the fifth. So the Bhatts aren't Bhagats from distant centuries. Tradition places them in the time of Guru Arjan, looking at the line of Gurus and singing what they saw. And what they saw was one light. One poet, Bhatt Mathura, lays it out in a single verse, in paraphrase: the Lord, in the form of light, was called Guru Nanak; from him came Angad, essence merged with essence; Angad set Amar Das firm; Amar Das gave Ram Das the royal canopy; now see Guru Arjan, the fifth. Like a lamp lit from a lamp. Different bodies, the same light. Praise poetry can stop at the person: this king's sword, that king's wealth. The Bhatts do praise the Gurus warmly, their wisdom, their steadiness, their nearness to God. But underneath the praise is a claim that isn't about any one person at all. It's about what passes between them. Sikh readers hear these verses as a witness, from outside the family, to the teaching that the Guru is one, whatever body the light is in. And this week has been a walk through the Granth's other voices. Sadhna pleading for grace. Ramanand at home in a house colored with love. Parmanand asking what the hearing was for. Surdas and his one line. Jaidev, the old poet. Bhikhan's medicine. And now the Bhatts, who brought their trade of praise to the Gurus and used it to point at the light.
screen: `SWAYYE: VERSES OF PRAISE, GURU BY GURU.` · `ONE LIGHT, LAMP FROM LAMP.` · `NOT THE PERSON: WHAT PASSES BETWEEN.` · `A WEEK OF OTHER VOICES.` · then, large: `POETS OF PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: praise someone's goodness. In the sit, bring to mind one person whose goodness you've seen up close. Not their looks or their success. Their goodness: patience, honesty, a kindness nobody noticed. Like a Bhatt, be specific. Find the exact moment you saw it. Then look for what's underneath it, the light in them that isn't only theirs. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhatt. A bard, a poet of praise. In the Granth, the Bhatts' swayye praise the Gurus as one light passed from Guru to Guru.
Your line: poets of praise. Today, tell one person, specifically, the goodness you've seen in them. One true sentence is enough. Day seven hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: The Bhatts' swayye are read and sung in the Guru Granth Sahib like the rest of Gurbani, and Sikhs turn to them for the teaching that the light of Guru Nanak passed whole from Guru to Guru.

notes: Bhatts as hereditary bards who came to Guru Arjan's court: given as 'as tradition tells it'; confirm.
Swayye grouped by Guru from the first to the fifth (Swayye Mahalle Pehle ke ... Panjve ke): confirm.
Paraphrase that the light of Guru Nanak passed to Guru Angad and on (e.g. joti joti ralaaee themes): a Keeper may wish to cite a specific swayya.
'Lamp lit from a lamp' is the script's image, not a quotation.
'An early witness from outside the family' is an interpretive claim; confirm or soften.
